subject: science
passage: Each bottlenose dolphin develops its own signature whistle, a pattern of sound unlike that of any other dolphin in its group. Researchers who played recordings of these whistles found that a dolphin responded most strongly to a copy of its own. Some scientists describe the whistles as names, much as a person turns when called.
passage_b: Marine biologist Anwar Haddad finds the comparison with names tempting but overstated. A signature whistle is produced mostly by the dolphin itself, to announce who and where it is, whereas people rarely go around saying their own names. Other dolphins do sometimes copy a companion's whistle, but evidence that they use the copy to address that individual is still thin. The whistles identify, Haddad says, but it is not clear that they call.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the comparison of whistles to names in Text 1?

choices.A: By arguing that dolphins cannot tell one whistle from another
choices.B: By suggesting that dolphins use whistles only to warn one another of danger
choices.C: By claiming that every dolphin in a group shares the same whistle
choices.D: By accepting that the whistles identify individuals but doubting that they work like names

explanation.why: Text 1 reports that scientists describe signature whistles as names. Haddad calls the comparison "tempting but overstated": a whistle is mostly self-produced, and evidence that dolphins use copies to address others is "still thin." He concludes that the whistles "identify" but may not "call," which accepts part of Text 1 and doubts the rest.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 accepts that dolphins copy particular whistles, which requires telling them apart.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 says whistles announce identity and location; it never mentions danger.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Both texts treat each whistle as belonging to one dolphin.
explanation.D: Correct. Haddad agrees that whistles announce identity but doubts that they are used to address individuals the way names are.
